title: The readable invention
bodyMd:
A patent system is often described as an exchange: an inventor receives a temporary exclusive right in return for disclosing an invention. The description can make disclosure sound like a binary event. Either the document is public or it is not. But publication alone does not ensure that another practitioner can understand and use the information once the exclusive period ends. The distinction resembles the difference between depositing instructions in a public room and arranging them so that a relevant reader can follow them. Accessibility in the legal sense may be satisfied by permission to inspect, while accessibility in the practical sense also depends on organization and intelligibility. Neither sense should simply replace the other. A secret but clear account fails the public exchange, and an open but unusable account may fail its informational purpose. The quality of disclosure therefore concerns a relationship among the document, its availability, and its intended users.

A technically complete description may still be difficult to find, fragmented across related filings, or written in language that obscures the practical steps. Conversely, a concise document may be usable by a skilled reader even though it omits background knowledge that specialists already share. The relevant audience matters. A requirement that every member of the public reproduce a complex invention would be unrealistic; a requirement that an appropriately skilled practitioner can do so serves a different and more focused purpose.

This functional view of disclosure also changes how one evaluates quantity. A system producing more pages has not necessarily supplied more usable knowledge. Repetition can bury a crucial instruction, while a clear diagram can communicate a relationship that many paragraphs leave obscure. Nor can clarity be judged entirely without considering the field: a notation familiar in one technical community may be unintelligible in another.

The exchange account remains useful if disclosure is understood as an obligation to make a relevant kind of learning possible. This does not settle every dispute over the appropriate scope or duration of exclusive rights. It identifies a distinct question that should not be lost inside those disputes: what can a competent reader actually recover from the published material? The public value of disclosure depends not simply on opening a file, but on whether opening it provides a workable route from a protected claim to usable knowledge.
